findings.title: Local cache is set before the limit check, so a denied device is admitted on retry
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `localCache` *before* calling `anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store rejects the device with `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the cache entry remains for 29 minutes, so the very next request from the same device hits the cache, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, and `Authenticate` succeeds. The newly added device limit therefore only denies the first request from an over-limit device; a simple refresh grants anonymous access for the rest of the cache TTL. The cache should only be populated after a successful create/update (or the limit error should be cached as a negative result).

findings.title: Device limit is bypassed by omitting the device ID header
findings.body: `TagDevice` returns nil immediately when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is absent, and `Authenticate` only fails on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. Consequently the device limit is only enforced for clients that volunteer the header; any client (curl, scripts, a modified browser) that omits it gets anonymous access regardless of the configured limit. If `device_limit` is intended as an access/seat cap this makes it trivially bypassable; at minimum this should be documented or requests without a device ID should be rejected when a limit is configured.

findings.title: Check-then-insert race allows exceeding the device limit
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` performs a `COUNT(*)` and then, in a separate session, an upsert. Two concurrent requests for new devices can both observe `count < deviceLimit` and both insert, so the number of active devices can exceed the configured limit (by up to the number of concurrent first-time requests, across all Grafana instances). There is no transaction, lock, or conditional insert guarding the check-then-act. If the limit must be strict, the count and insert need to be done atomically (e.g. `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < ?` or a serverlock).

findings.title: rowsAffected==0 misreported as limit reached on MySQL for unchanged rows
findings.body: `updateDevice` treats `rowsAffected == 0` as `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. With the default go-sql-driver/mysql settings (no `clientFoundRows`), MySQL reports 0 affected rows when an UPDATE matches a row but changes no values. Since `updated_at` has second precision in MySQL, a repeat update of an existing known device within the same second with unchanged IP/UA (possible across multiple instances since the local cache is per-process) yields 0 affected rows and the legitimate, already-counted device is wrongly denied access. Prefer an existence check (SELECT) or distinguish matched vs changed rows.

findings.title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path for every anonymous request
findings.body: Previously device tagging ran in a detached goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout so DB latency never blocked anonymous authentication. This change makes `TagDevice` synchronous on every anonymous request: for each uncached device it now performs a `COUNT(*)` over `anon_device` (when a limit is set) plus an upsert before the identity is returned. On busy public dashboards with many distinct devices this adds DB round-trips and DB-dependent latency to the auth hot path, and a slow/unavailable DB now slows every anonymous request instead of just dropping telemetry. Consider keeping the write async when no limit is configured, or at least bounding the work (e.g. cache the count).

findings.title: Limit error is not an errutil error, giving users a generic failure
findings.body: `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is a plain `fmt.Errorf` error that is returned straight out of `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The authn service has no status/public-message information for it, so the end user receives a generic authentication failure with no indication that the anonymous device limit was hit, and operators cannot distinguish it in responses. Using an `errutil` error (e.g. `errutil.Forbidden` / `TooManyRequests` with a public message) would surface the cause correctly.

findings.title: Missing tests for service/client-level device limit enforcement
findings.body: No test exercises the new behaviour end-to-end: there is no test that `Anonymous.Authenticate` returns an error when the limit is reached, nor that a repeated request from a denied device is also rejected (which would have caught the local-cache bypass in `tagDeviceUI`), nor that an existing device is still admitted when the limit is reached. `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only covers the store layer with a limit of 1.

findings.title: Frontend type for anonymousDeviceLimit does not match what the backend sends
findings.body: `anonymousDeviceLimit` is declared as `number | undefined` and defaulted to `undefined`, but the backend DTO field is a non-omitempty `int64`, so the frontend always receives a number (0 when unset) and never `undefined`. The type suggests callers should handle an absent value when in practice they must treat 0 as "no limit". Either mark the Go field `omitempty` or type it as `number` and document that 0 means unlimited.
